title: Roddy Piper
wiki_lead:
Roderick George Toombs (April 17, 1954 – July 31, 2015), known by his ring name "Rowdy" Roddy Piper, was a Canadian professional wrestler and actor.
In professional wrestling, Piper was best known to international audiences for his work with the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) and World Championship Wrestling (WCW) between 1984 and 2000. Although he was Canadian, Piper was billed as coming from Glasgow, Scotland and was known for his signature kilt and bagpipe entrance music, in reference to his Scottish heritage. Piper earned the nicknames "Rowdy" and "Hot Rod" by displaying his trademark "Scottish" short temper, spontaneity, and quick wit. According to The Daily Telegraph, he is "considered by many to be the greatest 'heel' (or villain) wrestler ever".
As one of wrestling's most recognizable stars, Piper headlined multiple pay-per-view events, including the WWF and WCW's respective premier annual events, WrestleMania and Starrcade. He accumulated 34 championships and hosted the popular WWF/WWE interview segment "Piper's Pit", which facilitated numerous kayfabe feuds. In 2005, Piper was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame by Ric Flair, who dubbed him "the most gifted entertainer in the history of professional wrestling".
Outside of wrestling, Piper acted in dozens of films and TV shows. Most notably, he took the lead role of John Nada in the 1988 cult classic They Live, and a recurring role as deranged professional wrestler Da' Maniac on the FX comedy series It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia.

Early life
Roderick George Toombs was born in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, on April 17, 1954, the son of Eileen (née Anderson), a Scottish-Canadian and Stanley Baird Toombs, an Anglo-Canadian. He had family roots in British Columbia and Wisconsin, and was of partial Scottish descent on his mother's side. He was raised in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and attended Windsor Park Collegiate. His father was an RCMP officer while they lived in The Pas, Manitoba.
After being expelled from junior high school for having a switchblade and falling out with his father, Toombs left home and stayed in youth hostels. Several professional wrestlers hired him to run errands as he picked up odd jobs at nearby gyms. As a young man, he became proficient in playing the bagpipes, though he repeatedly stated that he was unsure exactly where he picked them up. His childhood and lifelong best friend was ex-NHL player Cam Connor.
Piper was an amateur boxer before he became a professional wrestler. He sometimes claimed to have won a Golden Gloves championship, though their lists of champions do not include any of his names. He was awarded a black belt in Judo from Gene LeBell.


Professional wrestling career

grok_lead: Roderick George Toombs (April 17, 1954 â July 31, 2015), better known by the ring name "Rowdy" Roddy Piper, was a Canadian professional wrestler, actor, and broadcaster celebrated as one of the greatest villains in professional wrestling history. Born in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Piper began wrestling professionally at age 15 after a youth marked by amateur boxing, judo, and bagpipe performances, eventually becoming a key figure in the 1980s boom of the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) through his charismatic heel persona, trash-talking style, and innovative interview segment Piper's Pit. Over a career spanning more than three decades, he won over 30 championships across promotions, headlined the inaugural WrestleMania event, and influenced generations of performers with his blend of brawling, showmanship, and cultural impact. Piper's early career took him through various North American territories in the 1970s, where he honed his skills as a babyface before embracing the antagonistic "Rowdy" character in the mid-1970s with NWA Hollywood Wrestling. He joined the WWF in 1984, quickly becoming the promotion's top heel amid the Rock 'n' Wrestling era, feuding intensely with stars like Hulk Hogan in events such as The War to Settle the Score (1985) and teaming with Paul Orndorff against Hogan and Mr. T at WrestleMania I. His Piper's Pit segments, famous for moments like smashing Jimmy "Superfly" Snuka with a coconut, elevated wrestling's entertainment value and drew celebrity crossovers, including Cyndi Lauper. In addition to his in-ring successâincluding victories for the WWF Intercontinental Heavyweight Championship against The Mountie in 1992, the WCW United States Championship, and the World Tag Team Championship with Ric Flair in 2006âPiper appeared in notable matches at multiple WrestleManias, such as his bout with Bret Hart at WrestleMania VIII and the Hollywood Backlot Brawl against Goldust at WrestleMania XII. Transitioning later in his career, he ventured into acting with roles in films like John Carpenter's They Live (1988), where he delivered the iconic line "I have come here to chew bubblegum and kick ass... and I'm all out of bubblegum," as well as television shows and voice work. Piper's WWE Hall of Fame induction in 2005 cemented his legacy as a pioneer who bridged sports entertainment and pop culture. Piper died of a pulmonary embolism at his home in Hollywood, California, on July 31, 2015, at age 61, leaving behind his wife Kitty and four children. His death prompted tributes from the wrestling world, highlighting his enduring influence on modern stars like Ronda Rousey and his role in making professional wrestling a mainstream phenomenon.
